title: Adding, removing or reordering a pedal before the amp rebuilds the NAM amp without its model; it falls back to heavy fuzz until the next edit
evidence: syncChain reuses a processor only when the same type sits at the same index (GuitarPedalChain.ts:116-125). Otherwise it creates a new one and disposes the old (134-139). PedalBlockDescriptor carries no block id (PedalProcessor.ts:25-30). GuitarBassView.addBlock inserts new pedals before the amp by default (`copy.splice(ampIdx, 0, block)`, 633-637), and remove and reorder (619-622, 647-654) also shift indices. A new NamAmpPedal has no model, so wireChain takes the classic path (NamAmpPedal.ts:260-269): driveValue 0.4 gives 5× pre-gain into a tanh curve with k=21 (lines 81, 92, 95-98, 24). The view's NAM restore effect (GuitarBassView.tsx:534-547) is declared before the syncChain effect (550-562). In the same commit it checks adapter.isNamLoaded() against the old, still-loaded amp and skips. It runs again only on the next chain or readyVersion change.
impact: Adding a pedal in its default position, or deleting or dragging one before the amp, silently swaps a clean NAM amp (e.g. 'Quartz') for heavy fuzz. It stays that way until the student touches another control, which then triggers a refetch, parse and audio-thread prewarm stall (-08). Every pedal after the insertion point is also rebuilt: LFO phases reset and a new wah rAF loop starts. The discarded worklets leak (-17).
recommendation: Add a stable block id to PedalBlockDescriptor and reuse processors through a Map from id to processor, rewiring only when the order changes. Keep the NAM engine and its model attached to the amp block id. Let NamAmpPedal resolve its namModelId itself so a recreated amp restores its model without a UI effect. While a model is loading, use a clean or bypass path instead of k=21 fuzz.
verifierNote: syncChain reuses a processor only on a same-index, same-type match (GuitarPedalChain.ts:119-125). addBlock splices new pedals before the amp (GuitarBassView.tsx:633-637), so the amp gets a fresh NamAmpPedal with no namNode. That pedal falls into the preGain→shaper path (NamAmpPedal.ts:260-269) at drive 0.4. The restore effect (534-547) runs before the syncChain effect (550-562) in the same commit, still sees the old amp's isNamLoaded() true, and returns early.
impactNote: syncChain reuses a processor only when the same type sits at the same index (GuitarPedalChain.ts:113-125) and otherwise creates a new one. Descriptors carry no id (PedalProcessor.ts:24-30). addBlock's default insertion is `copy.splice(ampIdx, 0, block)` (GuitarBassView.tsx:636), which pushes the amp to a new index, so a fresh NamAmpPedal with no model is created. Without a loaded namNode, wireChain takes the classic path (NamAmpPedal.ts:260-269). The amp's default params contain no `drive` (DEFAULT_CHAIN at GuitarBassView.tsx:375-391), so driveValue stays at 0.4: preGain is 5 (line 92) and the curve has k = 0.4×50+1 = 21 (line 24). The restore effect (534-547) runs before the sync effect (550-562) in the same commit, sees isNamLoaded() true on the old amp, and skips. The next trigger is the next chain change. Effect: a student adds a pedal and the clean NAM amp turns into heavy fuzz until they touch something else. That is directly audible, confusing ('the overdrive pedal broke my sound'), and happens through the most common action in the pedal UI. High is justified.
regressionRisks: Adding block ids changes the persisted guitarChain/vocalChain shape. Old saves need ids generated on load deterministically (not Date.now()+random on each mount as in GuitarBassView.tsx:435), or collab peers will diff on ids. Keep the field optional for backward compatibility. Processor reuse by id means a processor that moves position keeps its LFO and wah state; that is the intent, but rewiring must disconnect cleanly to avoid clicks (consider a short output ramp). If NamAmpPedal resolves its own model, the fetch/parse/prewarm path moves out of React. Keep the model cache module-level and dedupe concurrent loads. A clean or bypass fallback during loading changes the tone heard in the first few hundred ms after load. Undo of add or remove must restore the same id so the processor and model are reused.

title: Each guitar/bass NAM amp runs a full 'standard' WaveNet per sample in scalar JS on the audio thread, even on silence
evidence: All 23 bundled models use the NAM standard config: layer arrays of 16 and 8 channels, kernel 3, 10 dilations up to 512 each, 13,802 weights (checked in public/daw-assets/nam-models). nam-processor.js process() evaluates the whole network for every sample whenever its input has channels, with no silence gate (lines 520-541). processSample (305-450) works out to about 13.3k multiply-adds, 240 Math.tanh calls and 720 double-modulo ring-index computations per sample. GuitarFxAdapter keeps live input flowing into the chain even with monitoring off: muteGain at gain 0 stays connected (GuitarFxAdapter.ts:73-75, 222-225). The default chain is a NAM amp (GuitarBassView.tsx:375-391) and the first model auto-loads (498-531).
impact: Estimated at about 1.7M multiply-adds and 31k tanh calls per 128-sample render quantum: a large share of the 2.67 ms budget for one instance, on every guitar or bass track with an input device attached, even with nobody playing. A guitar plus bass project, or a student Chromebook, is a likely source of crackling and underruns across the whole mix. Not measured here; needs profiling.
recommendation: Profile with chrome://tracing (audio category). Add a silence gate: once input stays below about −90 dBFS for longer than the receptive field, output zeros and skip compute, then re-prime on signal. Evaluate WASM SIMD inference (the NAM core compiled to WASM), block-wise matrix processing, or lite/feather architectures for the default models. Consider capping simultaneous NAM instances or defaulting extra tracks to the classic amp.
verifierNote: nam-processor.js:520-541 calls engine.processSample for every sample whenever input channel 0 exists, with no silence gate. GuitarFxAdapter feeds channelGain→muteGain (gain 0 when not monitoring)→pedal chain (GuitarFxAdapter.ts:73-75, 222-225), so a muted but active input still delivers channels. The roughly 13k MAC per sample figure fits the standard WaveNet config. CPU impact is an unprofiled estimate, and it only applies to tracks whose NAM was loaded via the view (see -01).
impactNote: The architecture claims are accurate. nam-processor.js process() runs engine.processSample for every sample whenever an input is connected, with no silence gate (public/daw-assets/nam-processor.js:520-541). processSample is plain scalar JS over the WaveNet layer arrays (305+), and 23 bundled models ship. muteGain sits before the chain and stays connected at gain 0 (GuitarFxAdapter.ts:73-75, 222-225), so an armed-but-quiet input keeps feeding zeros that are fully processed. Two qualifiers. (1) Per audio-analysis-01, a NAM worklet exists only after the student has opened CONTROLS on that track in this session, so 'every guitar or bass track with an input device' overstates today's exposure. Once opened, though, it keeps running after the view closes. (2) The CPU numbers are estimates. Even so, about 1.7M multiply-adds plus about 31k tanh per 128-sample quantum in scalar JS on a Chromebook-class core is plausibly most or all of the 2.67 ms budget, and crackling across the whole mix is what a student would notice. High severity is plausible but needs profiling. The silence gate is cheap and fixes the idle case only. Real performance needs WASM/SIMD or lighter models.
regressionRisks: Silence gate: NAM has a long receptive field (dilations up to 512, about 1-2k samples). Gating must re-prime or keep feeding the ring buffer, or you get a click or transient on note onset. A threshold that is too high cuts reverb-like tails and soft playing. A WASM port must match the current JS numerics (gain compensation, outputCompensation) or saved tones will sound different. Capping NAM instances or falling back to the classic amp changes how existing projects sound, so it needs a visible indicator. Fixing audio-analysis-01 without this one increases total NAM load on project open, so sequence carefully.

title: Audio clips started mid-clip play ~100 ms ahead of the beat, and loop laps cut audio early, because immediate start/stop paths ignore Tone's lookAhead
evidence: useTransport.ts:64 calls `transport.start()`, which starts the transport at now() = currentTime + lookAhead (tone ToneWithContext.js:35-37). Tone's default lookAhead is 0.1 s (Context.js:80) and nothing in src changes it. For the clip under the playhead, AudioClipScheduler.startSourceNow uses `const now = ctx.currentTime;` (216) and `source.start(now, offsetSeconds, playDuration)` (258) with the offset for `position`. That is one lookAhead before the transport, MIDI and future clips reach that tick. Tone processes ticks up to now() (Clock.js:200-224) and emits 'loop' with the future tick time (Transport.js:119-127). The loop handler ignores that time (usePlaybackEngine.ts:845-905): it calls `audioClipScheduler.cancelAll()`, which runs AudioClipScheduler.ts:101-104 `source.stop()` immediately with no fade, and restarts clips that straddle the loop start via startSourceNow at currentTime. `allNotesOff()` in the same handler (847-849) is just as early.
impact: Pressing Play inside a recorded take makes it play about 100 ms ahead of the drums and MIDI for the whole clip, which is longer than a 16th note at 150 BPM. While looping, the last ~0.1–0.15 s of each lap's audio is chopped with a click, and clips that straddle the loop start replay early on every lap. Loop practice and punch-in recording feel broken.
recommendation: Give the scheduler explicit times. Start mid-clip sources at the transport's actual start time (the time passed to transport.start). Stop and restart at the time argument of the 'loop' event, with a 5–10 ms fade. Better still, re-arm straddling clips through Transport.schedule at loopStart so Tone supplies the correct time.
verifierNote: useTransport.ts:64 `transport.start()` starts at now() = currentTime + lookAhead, while startSourceNow uses `const now = ctx.currentTime` (AudioClipScheduler.ts:216) and `source.start(now, ...)` (258). Nothing in src changes lookAhead. The loop handler (usePlaybackEngine.ts:846-905) ignores the event time and calls cancelAll, which does `source.stop()` immediately (AudioClipScheduler.ts:100-104). It then restarts straddling clips via startSourceNow at currentTime.
impactNote: useTransport.ts:63-64 sets the ticks and calls transport.start() with no time, so Tone starts at now() = currentTime + lookAhead (0.1 s by default; nothing in src/daw changes lookAhead). The scheduling effect (usePlaybackEngine.ts:643-716) sends clips already under the playhead through startSourceNow, which uses `const now = ctx.currentTime` (AudioClipScheduler.ts:216) and `source.start(now, offsetSeconds, ...)` (258). Those clips therefore sound about 100 ms before the transport, MIDI Parts and metronome reach that tick. Resuming from pause mid-take is a very common flow, and a 100 ms flam against drums is clearly audible. The loop handler (usePlaybackEngine.ts:845-905) ignores Tone's event time. It calls cancelAll, which calls source.stop() immediately (AudioClipScheduler.ts:101-104), while the transport is still about a lookAhead before the audible loop end, so each lap's tail is cut with a click. It also calls allNotesOff early (847-849).
regressionRisks: Passing an explicit start time to transport.start(time) also moves the metronome, count-in hand-off and recordStartTick alignment (audio-core-14), so re-check recording placement. Stopping at the loop event's time needs per-source stop(time) plus a scheduled gain ramp. cancelAll is also used on Stop, which should stay immediate. If straddling clips are re-armed via Transport.schedule at loopStart, make sure they don't double-fire with the existing future-clip schedule. Releasing notes later in the loop handler could briefly overlap with notes that start at loopStart, so test sustained pads.

title: From the second loop lap on, trimmed clips play their trimmed-away start; per-clip gain is never applied
evidence: scheduleClip takes ten positional parameters, the last being `clipOffsetSeconds = 0` (AudioClipScheduler.ts:23-36). The Play path passes `clip.offsetSeconds ?? 0` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:705-716), but the loop handler's call stops after the fade arguments (881-891), so the offset falls back to 0. Dragging a clip's start edge sets offsetSeconds (Timeline.tsx:2432-2437). There is no gain parameter at all, even though AudioClip.gain is saved and synced (tracksSlice.ts:153-154, SessionSerializer.ts:320, YjsDocManager.ts:135) and renderProject.ts:12-13 claims 'per-clip gain (AudioClipScheduler)'.
impact: From the second lap on, a trimmed take restarts from the very start of the recording (the breath before the count-in, a false start) instead of the trim point. Live playback and the bounce, which does pass the offset (renderProject.ts:350), disagree. Any clip gain coming from saved or collab data is ignored.
recommendation: Replace the positional signature with an options object built from the clip (`{ buffer, clip, engine, fromTick, when, pedalInput }`) so offset, fades and gain can't be dropped. Apply clip.gain on the per-source gain node, and add a unit test for the loop path.
verifierNote: The loop handler's scheduleClip call stops at `clip.fadeOutTicks` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:881-891), so clipOffsetSeconds falls back to 0 (AudioClipScheduler.ts:35). The Play path (705-716) and renderProject.ts:350 do pass `clip.offsetSeconds ?? 0`. No code in src/daw applies clip.gain; it is only declared and serialized (tracksSlice.ts:154, YjsDocManager.ts:135), even though renderProject.ts:12-13 claims per-clip gain.
impactNote: The loop handler's scheduleClip call (usePlaybackEngine.ts:881-891) stops after clip.fadeOutTicks, so clipOffsetSeconds defaults to 0 (AudioClipScheduler.ts:33-35). The Play path (705-716) and the bounce (renderProject.ts:340-351) both pass `clip.offsetSeconds ?? 0`. Dragging a clip's start edge writes offsetSeconds (Timeline.tsx:2432-2437). From the second lap on, every front-trimmed clip in the loop region, whether straddling or upcoming, plays from the untrimmed start, so the trimmed-away breath or false start comes back. Looping a trimmed take is common, so users will hear it. The gain half of the finding has little user impact: AudioClip.gain exists (tracksSlice.ts:153-154) and is serialized and synced, but no UI writes it. Ignoring it is a parity and comment-accuracy issue, not something users hear today.
regressionRisks: An options-object refactor touches three callers: Play, loop and renderProject. Keep the default behavior for clips without offsetSeconds, which older saved projects have. If you start applying clip.gain, any legacy or collab data with gain values that were never audible will suddenly change level, so consider clamping, or apply gain only once a UI exists.

title: Seeking during playback never reschedules: old audio keeps playing, the new position is silent, automation is stale, and notes can hang
evidence: seekTo only sets `Tone.getTransport().ticks = t` and the store position (useTransport.ts:11-16). It runs during playback from ruler clicks and playhead drags (Timeline.tsx:2065, on every drag move; 2296; 2309), skip back/forward (TransportBar.tsx:208-257) and the piano roll (PianoRoll.tsx:1478, 1528). Scheduling only re-runs when [isReady, isPlaying] change (usePlaybackEngine.ts:643-744). AudioClipScheduler has no reschedule method: running sources keep going, and future clips fire at their own startTick. AutomationScheduler.ts:12-17 states that 'nothing reschedules on a mid-play seek … a FORWARD seek skips breakpoints'. MidiScheduler schedules note-on and note-off as separate events (MidiScheduler.ts:28-40), so jumping past a sounding note's off tick never releases it.
impact: Clicking the ruler or skipping to a marker while playing is the most common way to move around in BandLab, Soundtrap, Ableton and Logic. Here it causes doubled or misaligned audio, silence where a clip should play, wrong automation values, and droning notes until Stop.
recommendation: Add an engine-level `reschedule(fromTick, when)`: fade out running sources, send allNotesOff at `when`, restart clips that span fromTick with the correct offset, and re-anchor automation. Call it from seekTo while playing, or on Tone's 'ticks' event. During playhead drags, seek on release or at most every ~100 ms.
verifierNote: seekTo only sets `Tone.getTransport().ticks` and the store position (useTransport.ts:11-16). Scheduling re-runs only on [isReady, isPlaying] (usePlaybackEngine.ts:744). It is called mid-play from playhead drag on every move (Timeline.tsx:2065), skip back/forward (TransportBar.tsx:228,243,257) and the piano roll (PianoRoll.tsx:1478,1528). AutomationScheduler.ts:12-17 documents this limitation itself, and MidiScheduler creates separate on/off events (MidiScheduler.ts:28-40).
impactNote: seekTo (useTransport.ts:11-16) only sets Tone.getTransport().ticks and the store position. Clip and automation scheduling re-runs only when [isReady, isPlaying] change (usePlaybackEngine.ts:643-744), and the only transport listener in src/daw is 'loop' (usePlaybackEngine.ts:907). Tone's ticks setter (Transport.js:449-461) emits stop and start, but nothing here listens for them. Raw AudioBufferSourceNodes keep playing, clips that span the new position don't start, and MidiScheduler's separate on/off events (MidiScheduler.ts:28-40) leave notes hanging after a forward jump. seekTo is reachable during playback from ruler clicks and drags (Timeline.tsx:2065, 2296, 2309), skip back/forward (TransportBar.tsx:208-257) and the piano roll (PianoRoll.tsx:1478, 1528). Clicking the ruler while playing is an everyday navigation gesture, and doubled audio or droning notes are obvious.
regressionRisks: Rescheduling on every drag-move event would thrash: debounce, or seek on release. A reschedule must cancel and re-arm MIDI Parts, audio sources and automation without touching the metronome repeat, or it should fix the metronome at the same time (audio-core-05). Recording in progress should probably block seeking or end the take, otherwise recordStartTick and overwriteAudioRegion ranges go wrong. The auto-rewind seekTo after recording (usePlaybackEngine.ts:1139) runs when stopped and must stay a plain seek.

title: The metronome grid starts wherever Play was pressed: off-beat clicks after pause/resume, missing clicks on later loop laps, wrong accent
evidence: MetronomeEngine.ts:41 `let beatCounter = 0;` and 43-56 `Tone.getTransport().scheduleRepeat((time) => {...}, interval)` with no start time. Tone treats a missing start time as the current transport position (Transport.js:183-189 `time: new TransportTimeClass(this.context, startTime).toTicks()`; TimeBase.js:188-189 `_noArg()` → TransportTime.js:18-19 `this.context.transport.seconds`). On 'loopStart', TransportRepeatEvent._restart sets `_nextTick = this.floatTime` and only offsets when `ticks > this.time`. So after the loop wraps to a start point earlier than where Play was pressed, the next click waits until that original position. Accents come from a click counter (45-55), not the bar position, and setTimeSignature restarts the counter mid-play (24-26). The click goes into `audioEngine.getMasterGain()` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:752), i.e. through the master fader, master automation and the mastering chain. The count-in, by contrast, accents by `i % num` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:798-806).
impact: Resume from a pause in the middle of a beat and every click lands between beats. The 'beat 1' accent falls on whatever beat playback started. With a loop that starts earlier than the play position, the click disappears for that part of every lap. A master fade or master compressor fades or pumps the click. For a music-theory product (this file even encodes 6/8 accents), the metronome is unreliable.
recommendation: Use `scheduleRepeat(cb, interval, 0)` and compute the beat number from `transport.getTicksAtTime(time)` inside each callback. Route the click through its own gain straight to the output with a user volume control, and share the accent logic with the count-in.
verifierNote: MetronomeEngine.ts:43-56 calls `scheduleRepeat(cb, interval)` with no start time, so TransportTime._noArg returns `this.context.transport.seconds` (TransportTime.js `_now`), which is the play position. TransportRepeatEvent._restart resets `_nextTick = this.floatTime` and offsets only when `ticks > this.time` (lines 83-93), so laps that wrap to before the start wait. The accent uses a counter (`beatCounter`, lines 41-55), and the click goes into getMasterGain (usePlaybackEngine.ts:752).
impactNote: MetronomeEngine.start (MetronomeEngine.ts:41-56) calls scheduleRepeat(cb, interval) with no start time. Tone anchors the grid at the current transport position, and accents come from a local beatCounter that starts at 0, so 'beat 1' is wherever Play was pressed. After pausing mid-beat (pause keeps the position, useTransport.ts:66-68), resuming makes every click land off the grid. Starting from bar 3 beat 2 puts the accent on beat 2. The effect at usePlaybackEngine.ts:747-764 also restarts the counter through setTimeSignature/setEnabled/start. Tone's repeat events do not fire before their start time, so with a loop that starts earlier than the play position, clicks are missing until the original start tick. The count-in, by contrast, accents by beat index (usePlaybackEngine.ts:798+). For a music-education product, a metronome that clicks off the beat is very noticeable. The claim about routing through the master gain and mastering chain is accurate (752) but secondary.
regressionRisks: scheduleRepeat(cb, interval, 0) with the beat computed from transport.getTicksAtTime(time) must use the time-signature-aware ticks per bar (denominator 8 or 2) to keep the 6/8 compound accents. Moving the click off the master gain changes its relative volume, and master-volume automation will no longer affect it. Some users may rely on the master fader to quiet the click, so add a click volume control. Make sure the export path, which creates its own transport, never schedules the metronome.

title: Undo brings back audio clips whose buffers were already evicted: they are silent, and unrecoverable if they were never uploaded
evidence: Buffers are evicted at edit time: overwriteAudioRegion.ts:66-67, 74-75 and 121; Timeline.tsx:1681 and 1966 (split) and 2016 (context-menu delete); useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:399 (Delete key). Undo snapshots and restores only tracks, chords and marks (undoMiddleware.ts:111-127); the AudioBufferStore (AudioBufferStore.ts:19) is outside undo history. Audio is downloaded again only for clips that have an assetId (useCollabAudioLoader.ts:30-33 → load-audio.ts:74).
impact: Delete, split or record over a clip, then press Cmd+Z, and the clip comes back silent. Uploaded clips show 'Loading…' until they download again. Split halves, overwrite remainders, takes whose upload failed and all guest audio stay silent for good. Undoing a bad punch-in, exactly when people rely on undo most, can lose the good take.
recommendation: Stop evicting buffers at edit time. Reference-count buffers per asset and evict only when neither the current project nor the undo/redo stacks reference them, or on project switch. Non-destructive split and overwrite (audio-core-06) removes most of the copies anyway.
verifierNote: Undo captures and restores only tracks, chordRegions and marks (undoMiddleware.ts:110-127). Buffers are evicted at edit time in Timeline.tsx:1681,1966,2016, useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:399 and overwriteAudioRegion.ts:66-67,74-75,121. The loader refetches only clips with an assetId (useCollabAudioLoader.ts:30-33), so restored split, remainder or never-uploaded clips stay silent.
impactNote: Deleting a clip evicts its buffer and original bytes immediately: useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:399, Timeline.tsx:2016, Timeline split at 1681/1966, and overwriteAudioRegion.ts:66-67/74-75/121. Undo restores only tracks, chordRegions and marks (undoMiddleware.ts:110-126), and the AudioBufferStore is a module-level Map outside history. useCollabAudioLoader.ts:30-33 re-fetches only clips that have an assetId. Delete then Cmd+Z is one of the most common editing gestures. Uploaded clips come back showing 'Loading…' until they download again. Split halves, overwrite remainders, failed uploads and guest audio stay silent for good. Undoing a bad punch-in, which is exactly when users reach for undo, can lose the good take. Users will notice and lose work.
regressionRisks: Keeping buffers alive raises memory pressure (see audio-core-08), so reference counting or eviction on project switch is required. Undo stacks hold up to 50 snapshots, so tie the lifetime of buffers referenced only by undo to the stack size. Collab: undo is local, but restored clip ids must still map to buffers on peers. Make sure resetUndoHistory, called in SessionSerializer.ts:628/677/794, also releases undo-only references.

title: Decoded audio is never cleared between projects, and every cloud open creates new clip ids, so audio piles up in memory for the whole session
evidence: clearAudioBuffers (AudioBufferStore.ts:74-77) is never called anywhere in src; entries are only removed by removeAudioBuffer during edits. deserializeCloudProject gives every audio clip `id: crypto.randomUUID()`, with the comment 'The AudioBufferStore is keyed on this' (SessionSerializer.ts:583-592), so reopening the same project decodes and stores another full copy. Decoded audio is 32-bit float per channel; a 3-minute stereo stem at 48 kHz is about 69 MB. Split and overwrite add full copies via sliceBuffer (AudioBufferStore.ts:80-98). Recordings also keep the compressed original (setOriginalAudio), and AudioRecorder keeps its chunk array until the next recording starts (AudioRecorder.ts:12, 46).
impact: Opening a few audio-heavy projects or demos, or the same project several times, adds hundreds of MB that are never freed. On 4 GB school Chromebooks this ends in a tab crash that takes unsaved work with it.
recommendation: Clear the buffer store and the pitch-buffer cache on New, Open, template and demo load, next to resetUndoHistory. Key decoded audio by assetId, which stays the same across opens, and have clips reference shared buffers. Release AudioRecorder's chunks after stop.
verifierNote: clearAudioBuffers (AudioBufferStore.ts:74-77) has no caller anywhere in src, and deserializeCloudProject assigns `id: crypto.randomUUID()` to each audio clip (SessionSerializer.ts:584-588), so each reopen decodes under new keys. Only pitchBufferCache is evicted for absent clips (usePlaybackEngine.ts:399-408). One minor detail is off: a new AudioRecorder is created for each take and the ref is set to null after stop (usePlaybackEngine.ts:1069), so its chunks are garbage-collected rather than kept until the next take.
impactNote: clearAudioBuffers is never called anywhere in src (a grep finds only its definition). deserializeCloudProject assigns `id: crypto.randomUUID()` to every audio clip (SessionSerializer.ts:584-588), and the store is keyed by clip id, so each re-open of the same project decodes and keeps another full float32 copy plus the compressed original. The teacher flow of opening many student projects in one tab, or a student opening several demos, grows memory without bound. At about 30-70 MB per decoded multi-minute stem, a few audio-heavy opens reach the gigabyte range and a Chromebook tab crash, taking unsaved work with it. The impact depends on how many audio-heavy projects are opened, but the teacher-review path makes it realistic.
regressionRisks: Clearing on New/Open must happen before the new project's loaders run, or freshly fetched buffers get wiped (a race with loadCloudProjectAudio). Clearing must also not drop buffers still in use by an in-progress upload (setOriginalAudio bytes for unsaved takes) when the user cancels a project switch. Keying by assetId changes how Timeline, the scheduler and pitchBufferCache look up buffers, which is a wide refactor. Collab peers resolve by clip id today. Clips without an assetId (fresh takes) still need clip-id keys.

title: Waveforms rescan every sample of every visible audio clip on each Timeline redraw, because computePeaks is uncached
evidence: computePeaks walks the whole requested window sample by sample (AudioBufferStore.ts:120-130) and reads only the left channel (109). Timeline.tsx:976-983 calls it inside draw() for every visible audio clip, over the clip's full playing window (previewOffsetSec to previewOffsetSec + previewDurationSec), not just the part on screen. draw() reruns whenever tracks, zoom, scrollLeft, selection, liveAudioPeaks or audioBufferVersion change (Timeline.tsx:1341-1365) and on every vertical-scroll frame (1369-1388). AudioBufferStore.emitChange notifies synchronously on every set and remove (25-27; Timeline subscriber at 446-451), and live recording peaks update every 66 ms (usePlaybackEngine.ts:1009-1026).
impact: A 3-minute stereo take is about 8.6 million samples per scan. With a few long clips on screen, every scroll or zoom frame and every clip-drag step spends tens of milliseconds here. The result is visible scroll and zoom jank, laggy clip drags, heavy load at 15 Hz while recording over existing audio, and one full redraw per decoded clip during project load. Stereo content panned hard right draws as flat.
recommendation: Build a min/max peak pyramid for each buffer once (in setAudioBuffer or a worker, covering both channels). Have computePeaks read the closest level for the visible range only, and batch store notifications to one per animation frame.
verifierNote: draw() calls computePeaks with the clip's full playing window (Timeline.tsx:976-983), and computePeaks walks every sample in that range, left channel only (AudioBufferStore.ts:109,120-130). Clips are culled horizontally (Timeline.tsx:895) but there is no peak cache. draw reruns on tracks, zoom, scrollLeft, selection, liveAudioPeaks (written every 66 ms while recording, usePlaybackEngine.ts:1009-1025) and audioBufferVersion (1342-1365), and on every vertical-scroll frame (1369-1388).
impactNote: computePeaks (AudioBufferStore.ts:101-135) scans every sample of the requested window on channel 0 with no caching. Timeline.tsx:976-983 calls it inside draw() for every visible audio clip, over the clip's whole playing window, not just the part on screen. A 3-minute take at 48 kHz is about 8.6M samples per clip per draw. On a 4-core Chromebook that takes several to tens of milliseconds per clip, repeated on every redraw triggered by scroll, zoom, selection, drag or buffer-store change. With a few long stems on screen, scroll, zoom and clip drags will visibly stutter. The left-channel-only read is a minor accuracy point.
regressionRisks: A peak pyramid adds memory per buffer (small, about 1-2% of the decoded size at a 256-sample bucket). Invalidate it on buffer replace and pitch-shift (resolvePitchBuffer returns a different buffer). The draw must still honor offsetSeconds and trimmed windows. Batching store notifications to once per animation frame delays the first waveform paint slightly, so avoid a 'Loading…' flash. A worker-based build needs a transfer copy of the channel data.

title: Recorded takes land off the beat: there is no timestamp for when capture actually starts and no latency compensation
evidence: The new clip is placed at `recordStartTickRef.current`, the playhead position when recording began (usePlaybackEngine.ts:955, 971 → 1114-1117). For mic input, capture only starts after a fresh getUserMedia call resolves (1050-1054); the first take also waits on the permission prompt. For amp and vocal tracks capture starts immediately (1039-1043), about one lookAhead (0.1 s) before the transport reaches that tick (useTransport.ts:64). AudioRecorder.startRecording (AudioRecorder.ts:15-28) returns no timestamp and doesn't wait for `onstart`. Nothing subtracts output or input latency. AudioEngine exposes only baseLatency (AudioEngine.ts:188-190), which SettingsModal.tsx:108 displays as 'the latency', and the standardized-audio-context wrapper has no outputLatency. MidiRecorder compensates for lookAhead and event delay (MidiRecorder.ts:61-79) but not for the output latency the player is hearing.
impact: Mic takes land early by the time it takes to open the device, which differs on every take and is several seconds when the permission prompt shows. Amp and vocal takes land about 100 ms late. All audio and MIDI takes are also late by the output latency: 10–40 ms on wired output, 150–250 ms on the Bluetooth headphones many students use. Every take has to be nudged into place by hand.
recommendation: Open the input when a track is armed. Timestamp the first captured frame in AudioContext time (capture via AudioWorklet or MediaStreamTrackProcessor, or use onstart plus the native context's getOutputTimestamp) and place the clip at transport.getTicksAtTime(thatTime). Add a latency test or manual offset in Settings, as BandLab and Soundtrap have, and subtract outputLatency + inputLatency for audio and outputLatency for MIDI.
verifierNote: The clip is placed at recordStartTickRef, which is set from the position at start (usePlaybackEngine.ts:955,971,1114-1117). Mic capture begins only after getUserMedia resolves (1050-1054), while the adapter path starts immediately (1039-1043), about one lookAhead before the transport tick is heard (useTransport.ts:64). AudioRecorder.startRecording returns no timestamp and doesn't await onstart (AudioRecorder.ts:15-28), and no latency compensation exists.
impactNote: The clip is placed at recordStartTickRef, the playhead tick when recording begins (usePlaybackEngine.ts:955, 971), and later at startTick (1114-1117). For the mic path, getUserMedia is only called after recording starts (1050-1054), and MediaRecorder.start then begins capture (AudioRecorder.ts:15-28) with no timestamp. The take is therefore shifted early by the device-open time, which varies per take and is seconds on the first permission prompt. Amp and vocal adapter streams start recording immediately (1039-1043), while the transport starts about 0.1 s later (useTransport.ts:64), so those takes land late. No output or input latency compensation exists anywhere in src/daw (a grep for outputLatency or latency offset finds nothing). Students recording vocals or guitar to a beat will hear their takes off-time and have to nudge them by hand. That is clearly noticeable in a core flow, worse on Bluetooth headphones.
regressionRisks: Opening the mic on arm instead of on record changes permission-prompt timing and keeps the mic indicator on while a track is armed, which could surprise users and matter for school privacy. Shifting placement interacts with overwriteAudioRegion ranges, the 5-minute recording cap computation (computeMaxRecordSeconds) and the auto-rewind seekTo. A manual latency offset setting needs persistence per device, not per project. MIDI compensation in MidiRecorder.ts:61-79 must not double-subtract lookAhead.

title: The bundled reverb IR pack is marked PLACEHOLDER-DO-NOT-SHIP (derived from Logic Space Designer) and is served from public/
evidence: public/daw-assets/reverb-irs/manifest.json contains the warning 'CONTAINS PLACEHOLDER assets derived from reference (non-redistributable) IRs for local verification ONLY. Replace with licensed sources in pack-list.json and re-run pack before shipping.' Every entry has license 'PLACEHOLDER-DO-NOT-SHIP' and a sourceName such as 'Logic Space Designer — Fine Hall (reference)'. reverbIR.ts:32 fetches from '/daw-assets/reverb-irs/', which Vite copies into the build. Return A's reverb is on by default, so every Studio session downloads these files. There is no pack-list.json or pack script in the repo.
impact: Shipping IRs that may not be redistributed is a licensing risk. Removing them without a replacement silently switches every reverb to the synthetic generator: a different sound, plus the main-thread and memory costs described in audio-core-16.
recommendation: Replace them before release with licensed or CC0 IRs (or self-recorded ones). Add a build check that fails if any license says PLACEHOLDER, and make the synthetic fallback cheap (bounded cache, generated off the main thread).
verifierNote: public/daw-assets/reverb-irs/manifest.json has `_warning: "CONTAINS PLACEHOLDER assets derived from reference (non-redistributable) IRs..."`, and every entry shown has `license: "PLACEHOLDER-DO-NOT-SHIP"` and a sourceName such as "Logic Space Designer — Fine Hall (reference)". reverbIR.ts:32 fetches from '/daw-assets/reverb-irs/', the five WAVs are present in public/, and no pack-list.json exists in the repo. title: Autosave never fires during playback and is cancelled on unmount; the next param-less boot restores the older autosave over newer work
evidence: useAutosave.ts:19-25 subscribes to every store change: `useStore.subscribe(() => { if (timer != null) clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => { writeLocalSession(); ... }, AUTOSAVE_DEBOUNCE_MS) })` (1500 ms). While playing, useTransport.ts:79-93 calls setPosition every ~33 ms (transportSlice.ts:201 `set({ position: ... })`), so the timer is reset ~30x/s and never elapses. On unmount useAutosave.ts:27-30 clears the pending timer without writing; writeLocalSession is only called from useAutosave.ts:22 and there is no pagehide/beforeunload handler in src/daw or src/lib/studio-projects. On the next mount without a boot param ("Continue last session" → StudioNewProject.tsx:55 `navigate(StudioRoutes.editor.definition)`, or browser Back to the param-stripped URL), DawApp.tsx:425-428 runs `restoreLocalSessionIfPresent()`, which deserializes the older localStorage copy over the newer in-memory singleton store (localSession.ts:43-48; SessionSerializer.ts:764 also restores its projectId).
impact: Editing while a loop plays is the core DAW workflow. A student who tweaks a loop and then refreshes, crashes, or navigates to Learn/Home while it is still playing (or within 1.5 s of an edit) silently loses every change since pressing Play — reload kinds (a) and (d). UI-only store churn (selection, zoom) also keeps postponing the write.
recommendation: Subscribe with a selector over persisted fields only (tracks, chordRegions, bpm, key/mode, markers, returns, mastering, projectName…) via subscribeWithSelector + shallow equality, so position/UI updates never reset the debounce. Flush synchronously on unmount, `pagehide` and `visibilitychange: hidden`. Store an editRevision/timestamp with the autosave and, on a param-less boot, keep the in-memory session when it is newer instead of restoring over it.
verifierNote: useAutosave.ts:19-25 resets a 1500 ms debounce on every store change, and useTransport.ts:79-90 calls setPosition (transportSlice.ts:201 `set({ position })`) about every 33 ms while playing, so nothing is written until playback stops plus 1.5 s. The unmount cleanup (useAutosave.ts:27-30) clears the timer without writing, writeLocalSession has no other caller, and there is no pagehide/beforeunload handler. A param-less boot then runs restoreLocalSessionIfPresent() (DawApp.tsx:425-428 → localSession.ts:43-48), which writes the stale copy over the in-memory singleton, projectId included (SessionSerializer.ts:764). This is real data loss in the core edit-while-looping flow.
impactNote: The mechanism checks out. useAutosave.ts:19-25 subscribes to the whole store and restarts a 1500 ms timer on every change. useTransport.ts:72-93 calls setPosition about every 33 ms while playing, so the timer never fires during playback. The cleanup at useAutosave.ts:27-30 clears the pending timer without writing. The only writeLocalSession caller is the autosave hook, and grep finds no beforeunload/pagehide handler in src/daw or src/lib/studio-projects (AudioEngine.ts:97 listens to visibilitychange for audio only). On a param-less boot, DawApp.tsx:428 calls restoreLocalSessionIfPresent(), and localSession.ts:43-48 deserializes the older copy over the in-memory singleton store, so 'Continue last session' (StudioNewProject.tsx:55) after an SPA hop can roll back newer in-memory work. Downgraded from critical to high because the loss window is narrow. Stopping playback changes isPlaying and the write lands 1.5 s later. So work is lost only when the student edits while a loop plays, then reloads, closes the tab or leaves the editor without pressing Stop (or within 1.5 s of an edit). That does happen in loop-based work, and the loss is silent. No continuous store writers were found while stopped, so autosave does work outside playback.
regressionRisks: Persisting through a selector needs a list of persisted fields that matches SessionSerializer. If a field is missing from the list, its edits never trigger a save. That list has to be kept in sync as new fields are added to the serializer. subscribeWithSelector may require wrapping the store's middleware stack, which interacts with undoMiddleware order. A synchronous flush on pagehide or unmount serializes the whole project on the main thread, which can be slow for large projects, and a localStorage quota failure must not throw. Skipping the restore when the in-memory copy is newer must not interfere with the collab rejoin branch (DawApp.tsx:384-390), ?seeded=1 song handoff, or tutorial boot. It also must never revive a stale room state. Saved-project format is unaffected unless an editRevision field is added; if one is added, readers must tolerate its absence.

title: Nothing loads until the first click, and the first Play starts the transport before any instrument is ready, with no feedback
evidence: initEngine runs only from a one-shot document click/keydown listener (DawApp.tsx:437-448). All TrackEngine/instrument creation, and therefore every sample fetch, is gated by `if (!isReady) return;` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:379-381). Instruments attach only after async init (`instrument.init(...).then(() => { trackEngine.setInstrument(instrument)`, :508-511); until then TrackEngine.noteOn is `this.instrument?.noteOn(...)` (TrackEngine.ts:73-74) and samplers return early while `!this.loaded`. TransportBar's withInit calls `onInit()` without awaiting and then runs the action (TransportBar.tsx:193-199). useTransport therefore starts Tone.Transport at once (useTransport.ts:56-64), while the schedule effect (usePlaybackEngine.ts:643-744) only runs after isReady flips, into instruments that are still downloading. Drum readiness is tied to every download in the app: loadKit awaits `Tone.loaded()` per pad (DrumMachineEngine.ts:168-176), which loops over the global ToneAudioBuffer.downloads list (tone/build/esm/core/context/ToneAudioBuffer.js `static loaded()`). Drums therefore wait for the slowest sampler, third-party CDNs included, and the drum load rejects if any other download fails. The click also synchronously builds 3 + N EffectChains (AudioEngine.ts:32-49, TrackEngine.ts:26). Each one gives its ConvolverNode a 2 s stereo IR (EffectChain.ts:512-517) even though reverb is off by default (DEFAULT_EFFECTS.reverb.enabled=false, :148-149). No loading UI exists: subscribeEngineReady is only consumed by OrganView, VocalView and GuitarBassView.
impact: Opening a demo or template and pressing Play — the first thing a student does — plays silence or a partial mix for as long as tens of MB take to download (see -04/-05). The playhead moves and nothing explains why. The same happens after every return to the editor, because engines are rebuilt (-13).
recommendation: Decouple loading from the gesture: create the engine graph and instruments on the suspended Tone context at mount and start fetch+decode immediately (decodeAudioData works on a suspended context); the first gesture only resumes. Keep per-track readiness in the store. Make Play wait (up to a timeout) for audible tracks, with a white/10 transport pill "Loading sounds · 2/4" and a per-track spinner in TrackHeader (aria-busy + polite live region). Replace `await Tone.loaded()` with awaiting each Player's own buffer. Only assign reverb IRs once reverb is enabled.
verifierNote: initEngine only runs from a one-shot document click/keydown listener (DawApp.tsx:437-448), and useAudioEngine resets isReady to false on every mount. Track engines are gated by `if (!isReady) return;` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:379-380), and instruments attach after an async init().then (:508-511). TransportBar's withInit calls onInit() without awaiting it before running the action (TransportBar.tsx:193-199). DrumMachineEngine awaits the global `Tone.loaded()` for each pad (DrumMachineEngine.ts:172-173), and every EffectChain synthesises a reverb IR even though reverb defaults to disabled (EffectChain.ts:148-149, 512-517).
impactNote: Engine init is gated on the first document click or keydown (DawApp.tsx:437-448). initEngine is async (useAudioEngine.ts:13-23), and withInit fires onInit() without awaiting it, then runs the action (TransportBar.tsx:193-198). Track and instrument creation is gated by `if (!isReady) return;` (usePlaybackEngine.ts:379-381), and each instrument attaches only after its async init resolves (usePlaybackEngine.ts:508-511). DrumMachineEngine.loadKit awaits the global Tone.loaded() per pad (DrumMachineEngine.ts:168-176), so drums wait on every outstanding ToneAudioBuffer download, including the 17 bass MP3s, and fail if any of those fail. EffectChain builds a ConvolverNode with a generated IR at construction even though reverb is off (EffectChain.ts:512-517). Loading-state consumers are limited to OrganView, VocalView and GuitarBassView (plus internal hooks), and nothing appears in the transport bar or track headers. On a cold cache, combined with the 19.5 MB kit (-04) and the 31 MB SF2 (-05), the first Play on a template or demo is silent or partial for seconds while the playhead moves. Students will notice this on their first interaction.
regressionRisks: Creating the graph before the gesture means an AudioContext in the suspended state. Chrome allows that, but Tone.start()/resume must still run on the gesture, and any code that assumes getIsInitialized() means 'running' must be checked. SoundFontAdapter's initSharedSynth resumes the context itself (SoundFontAdapter.ts:220-224), which must not run before a gesture. Making Play wait for readiness changes transport timing: collab transportSync followers must not desync when one peer is still loading. Prefer starting the transport and muting, or block only locally. Assigning reverb IRs lazily needs the enable path to set convolver.buffer before routing wet signal, or toggling reverb on can click or produce silence. Replacing Tone.loaded() with per-Player loading changes the last-wins kit-swap logic (loadSeq) and must keep disposing discarded players.

title: Default 'Natural' drum kit is 19.5 MB of 24-bit stereo WAV, decoded separately for every drum track
evidence: 11 files of 1.44–2.51 MB each (kick.wav 1,440,080 B; ride.wav 2,512,592 B). The WAV fmt chunk reads PCM, 2 ch, 48 kHz, 24-bit, so the kick and snare are 5 s long, the crash 8.0 s and the ride 8.7 s. The 808 kit covers the same 11 pads in 0.78 MB (mono, 16-bit). 'natural' is the default (`private currentKit: DrumKitId = 'natural'`, DrumMachineEngine.ts:67; `track.drumKit ?? 'natural'`, usePlaybackEngine.ts:431). All 4 templates contain a drum-machine track without a kit (projectTemplates.ts:36,70,110,150), and all 3 demos add one (applyDemoDrums.ts:33 `store.addTrack('midi', 'drum-machine', 'Drums')`). Each engine does `new Tone.Player(url)` (DrumMachineEngine.ts:172), and Tone's ToneAudioBuffer.load fetches and decodes per instance with no URL cache. Each drum track therefore holds its own float32 copy (~3.24 M frames × 2 ch × 4 B ≈ 26 MB), re-decoded on every editor remount.
impact: About 20 MB must download before the drums sound on any template or demo. Each drum track also uses about 26 MB of RAM and causes a large decode burst, which hurts most on the low-end Chromebooks common in schools.
recommendation: Re-master the kit: trim tails (drums ≤1.5–2 s, cymbals ≤4 s), 16-bit, mono where the source is mono, then compress (Opus/AAC/MP3 ~160 kbps, or FLAC); target ≤2 MB. Add a module-level Map<url, Promise<AudioBuffer>> decode cache (like reverbIR.ts nativeCache) that all DrumMachineEngine/sampler instances share, survives remounts and has an LRU byte cap.
verifierNote: The 11 natural-kit files total about 19 MB (ls: kick.wav 1,440,080 B; ride.wav 2,512,592 B). The fmt chunk reads PCM, 2 ch, 0xBB80 = 48 kHz, 24-bit, and the kick's data chunk is 1,440,000 B, which is 5 s. 'natural' is the default (DrumMachineEngine.ts:67; usePlaybackEngine.ts:431). The templates (projectTemplates.ts:36,70,110,150) and applyDemoDrums.ts:32 all create drum-machine tracks, and each pad is a separate `new Tone.Player(url)` with no shared decode cache.
impactNote: File sizes are as stated: public/daw-assets/samples/drums/natural holds 11 WAVs of 1.44 to 2.51 MB, about 19.5 MB in total. 'natural' is the default kit (DrumMachineEngine.ts:67; usePlaybackEngine.ts:431). All four templates include a drum-machine track (projectTemplates.ts:36,70,110,150), and demos add one via applyDemoDrums. Each pad does `new Tone.Player(url)` (DrumMachineEngine.ts:172) with no shared decode cache. That is the largest download on the path to the first audible drum beat, and the decode costs roughly 26 MB of float32 per drum track. Browser HTTP caching softens repeat visits, though decoding still repeats on every remount. Most projects have one drum track, so the RAM figure is per project, not multiplied. High is fair because this is a big part of why -03 is so noticeable on a cold cache.
regressionRisks: Re-mastering changes how the kit sounds. Trimmed cymbal tails or a switch to mono will be audible in existing student projects, so keep the kit id 'natural' and keep pad mapping and note numbers unchanged so saved projects still load. Changing config.ext (wav to mp3/ogg) needs format support: Opus in Safari is shaky, so MP3 or AAC is safer. Lossy encoders add leading padding that shifts drum transients a few ms. Trim it, or use FLAC or a 16-bit WAV. A shared decode cache must hand out the same AudioBuffer read-only. Players must not mutate it, and the LRU must not evict buffers still in use by a live Player. Offline render (renderProject.ts) must also resolve through the cache.

title: A 30 MB GM SoundFont gates every demo's bass and 17 of 27 instrument presets; a failed load is permanent and silent
evidence: initSharedSynth loads a 380 KB worklet (10 s timeout), then `fetch('/daw-assets/GeneralUser_GS.sf2')` (30 MB) and addSoundBank (SoundFontAdapter.ts:226-259). title: Server-message listener is attached only to the first WebSocket, so it's lost after any reconnect

title: Note edits replace the whole Y.Array on every mouse move

title: Meters set React state at 60fps per track and keep polling when stopped; the mastering 'LUFS' value is a relabelled peak reading
evidence: useMeterLevel.ts:24-45 runs a never-ending animation-frame loop per analyser: it reads getByteTimeDomainData and calls setLevel() every frame. It is used per track in TrackHeader.tsx:91-93, so each 80px header (motion.div plus Radix Popover and Slider) re-renders up to 60 times a second during playback. It is also used per strip (StudioView.tsx:616) and for master L/R (MasterTrackHeader.tsx:50-51; StudioView.tsx:194-195 and 762-763). MeterBar keeps its peak hold in React state (StudioView.tsx:438-455). SpectrumAnalyzer measures its container once (StudioView.tsx:55-60, no resize handling) and draws every frame even when stopped (95-164). LufsMeter (StudioView.tsx:198) computes `const lufs = avg > 0 ? -14 + (avg / 100) * 14`: a peak level mapped linearly onto -14…0 and labelled 'LUFS' (231-241). That makes three meter implementations, plus a dead fourth (Mixer/ChannelStrip MeterSegments).
impact: With 8 tracks, the CREATE view does about 480 header renders per second on top of the 30Hz position updates. That main-thread load competes with audio scheduling and input. The analyser loops keep running when idle. The MASTER view shows students an invented loudness number.
recommendation: Build one Meter primitive. Draw it on canvas (or via a CSS custom property) updated from refs, not React state. Drive all meters from one shared MeterBus animation frame that runs only while the transport plays or a level is still decaying, and pauses when hidden. Keep peak hold inside the canvas. Size the spectrum with a ResizeObserver and pause it when stopped. Relabel the meter 'Peak dBFS', or implement real short-term LUFS (K-weighting plus gating).

StudioView.tsx:55-60 measures the spectrum once and its draw loop never stops. Line 198 computes `-14 + (avg/100)*14` from a peak level and labels it 'LUFS', so that number is invented.
impactNote: useMeterLevel.ts:24-45 runs an endless requestAnimationFrame loop per analyser and calls setLevel every frame. It is used per track in TrackHeader.tsx:91-93, per MixingStrip (StudioView.tsx:616), for the master L/R in MasterTrackHeader.tsx:50-51, StudioView.tsx:194-195 and 762-763, and also in Mixer/MixerPanel.tsx:24-25 and Mixer/ChannelStrip.tsx:149. During playback the rounded level changes almost every frame, so each TrackHeader re-renders at about 60fps. That is a heavy component: motion buttons, a Radix Slider, a Popover. MasterStrip (StudioView.tsx:757-765) re-renders at 60fps too and also subscribes to tracks. With 8 tracks this is hundreds of React renders per second, on top of the playhead updates, for the whole time audio plays: continuous main-thread load on the target Chromebooks. When stopped the cost drops sharply. The level decays to 0, and React bails out of identical setState calls, so idle cost is just the rAF loop plus a 256-sample getByteTimeDomainData (fftSize 256 in TrackEngine.ts:30 and AudioEngine.ts:56-60). The 'keeps polling when stopped' part is therefore minor. The LUFS claim is exact: StudioView.tsx:198 computes `-14 + (avg / 100) * 14` from peak levels and labels it 'LUFS' (231-241). regressionRisks: Moving meters to canvas or CSS variables driven from refs removes React-rendered segment divs, so any tests asserting meter DOM (MeterSegments / data attributes) need updating. A shared MeterBus that pauses when the transport stops must still run for live input monitoring and recording (armed tracks with monitoring on and transport stopped) and for collab remote audio (useRemoteTrackActivity), or meters will look dead while the student is playing in. title: Autosave never runs during playback, so edits made while a loop plays are lost on refresh or crash (cross-slice)
evidence: useAutosave.ts:19-25 subscribes to every store change, with no selector, and restarts a 1,500ms timer (AUTOSAVE_DEBOUNCE_MS, line 8) on each one. useTransport.ts:80-89 calls setPosition every 33ms or more while playing, and transportSlice.ts:201 `setPosition: (tick) => set({ position: … })` is a store change. The timer is therefore reset about 30 times a second and can never fire during playback. writeLocalSession is called only from useAutosave.ts:22 (grep): there is no flush on pagehide, visibilitychange or beforeunload, and the cleanup (27-30) drops a pending save.
impact: Drum programming, groove loading, piano-roll edits, pad-mix and organ changes are usually made while a loop plays. All of them live only in memory until 1.5 s after the student presses Stop. An accidental refresh, a tab crash or a closed laptop lid during playback restores the session as it was before playback (reload type a), silently, losing minutes of work.
recommendation: Subscribe with a selector over persisted state only (tracks, chord regions, marks, bpm/key/time signature, returns, mastering…), so position and UI changes don't reset the debounce. Add a maximum wait (flush at least every ~5 s while there are unsaved changes), and flush on pagehide, on visibilitychange=hidden and when the editor unmounts.
verifierNote: useAutosave.ts:19-25 subscribes to the whole store with no selector and restarts a 1500ms timer on every change. useTransport.ts:80-89 calls setPosition (transportSlice.ts:201) every 33ms or more while playing, so the timer never fires during playback. Grep shows writeLocalSession is called only from useAutosave.ts:22, with no pagehide/visibilitychange/beforeunload flush, and the cleanup clears the pending timer.
impactNote: useAutosave.ts:19-25 subscribes to the whole store and clears the 1.5s timer on every change. useTransport.ts:80-89 calls setPosition about every 33ms while playing (transportSlice.ts:201 is a plain set), so the timer can never fire during playback. writeLocalSession is called only from useAutosave.ts, nothing flushes on pagehide or beforeunload, and the cleanup (27-30) discards a pending save. The loss is real but only happens when a refresh, crash or tab close comes during or right after playback. Pressing Stop saves the work 1.5s later. That makes it high rather than critical.
regressionRisks: A selector-based subscription has to cover every persisted field (tracks, chord regions, marks, tempo/key/time signature, returns, mastering, synth/organ per-track state held in other stores). Missing one would stop that field from autosaving. If the synth store is persisted separately, check that it still writes. A max-wait flush during playback runs writeLocalSession (serialization plus localStorage) on the main thread every ~5s, which could cause a small audio-UI hitch on Chromebooks. Keep it cheap or use requestIdleCallback. A pagehide flush must not run after File > New Project has cleared the session, or it would resurrect the old one.

title: The SoundFont panel waits behind a 31 MB download with no progress, and spins forever if loading fails
evidence: SoundFontView.tsx:63 starts with `useState(true)` and 66-91 polls `trackEngine.getInstrument()` every 200ms. While loading (176-189), the whole panel is replaced by 'Loading SoundFont...', including the General MIDI program list, which only needs the store (100-111). The adapter fetches `/daw-assets/GeneralUser_GS.sf2` (SoundFontAdapter.ts:246-253), which is 31,281,186 bytes in public/; the body read (`await sfResponse.arrayBuffer()`) is outside the 30 s timeout. On any failure, the rejected `synthInitPromise` is cached for good (SoundFontAdapter.ts:77-80, never reset), and usePlaybackEngine calls `trackEngine.setInstrument` only on success (~523), so the poll never ends. OrganView already avoids polling (OrganView.tsx:38-47).
impact: On a school network, the first General MIDI track shows a spinner for tens of seconds with no sign of progress. If the worklet or the download times out once, every SoundFont track shows 'Loading SoundFont...' for the rest of the session with no error or retry, and the student can't even pick a sound.
recommendation: Show the program list and keyboard immediately, with a progress bar over the keyboard only. Replace polling with subscribeEngineReady. Have the adapter expose its load state (percent, error), reset synthInitPromise on failure, and show 'Couldn't load sounds — Retry'. Cache the SF2 in Cache Storage. Consider a smaller General MIDI bank or loading programs on demand.
